doc.title: Red Holloway interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Recording sessions: Brother Jack McDuff's Live at the Front Room and John Mayall
summary: He scorns long studio overdubbing and describes how McDuff's and Mayall's bands rehearsed, played jobs, then recorded quickly.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Can you describe what a typical recording session might have been like for one of the blues artists? Because today we’re familiar with how bands sometimes spend weeks and months making records, and they make them in sections, and they overdub—
And they do the rhythm section first, they do the solo tracks after that, and all this intricate mixing.

That is so ridiculous. That is just really stupid. And I don’t care who hears it that’s stupid. That’s just a waste of time and money. The way we used to do, and the way I still do myself, is what I’ll do is like when I was working with Brother Jack McDuff, even John Mayall, now he’s a British, father of the British blues, I worked with him. We would rehearse the stuff at his house, all the changes that had to be made, then we would play it on some jobs. We’d play it maybe for a month. And I still do that, and McDuff. We’ll play our stuff for maybe 2-3 months and there would be, in fact, when I worked and made the first record for McDuff, him and George Benson and Joe Dukes had been playing together for oh a couple of years. And I had joined him like his saxophone player had to go down south because somebody had died in the family. And I joined his band, like at 3:00 that day and we rehearsed from 3 until about 6 the stuff that he was going to do. And we went to the studio and they had an audience and the audience had been drinking from 6 until 8, that’s when the session was starting. And basically everyone knew the music except myself, you know, but I went and rehearsed with him that day and I wrote down what I was playing, more or less the melodic lines, so it made it rather easy. Whereas George and McDuff was playing the harmony. So when we went to the session that night, it was perfect. The people, they had been, they got high and they had been drinking and eating barbecue ribs and just having a good time. So they were high and loose, and that was the album “Live at the Front Room.” And when it came out it was a hit. And that’s really what started the whole thing off. So like, even when I worked with John Mayall, we would practice the stuff and we’d play it on gigs, then we’d go in the studio and they’d take maybe 5 hours to do an album. But I mean this is stupid, going in, well they don’t, one of the thing is they don’t have anything prepared. That’s usually what it is. Most of the groups of today that tie up a studio for two and three months, cost $150,000-$200,000. That is stupid. And because usually most of them don’t really know anything about the instruments. In fact there was a girl’s group and they had this hit, and the fella who had them and was interviewing them and he said, “Well, now what is your

next thing that you’re going to do. You’ve got this big hit” whatever the name of it was. And so they say, “Well, we’re going to go in and try and learn how to play these instruments.” And I mean this was on television, and I said well I’ll be darned.
Well you know my daughter, she says like people are getting so accustomed to just mediocre stuff, they don’t know good shit when they hear it.
